claims.text: Localized residual stresses produced by thermal-expansion mismatch during solidification, together with intrinsic lattice distortions, dominate the stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-mismatch residual stresses govern behavior by altering dislocation dynamics and precipitation processes.
Conventional rapid cooling of as-cast HfNbTaTiZr naturally induces a heterogeneous microstructure and residual-stress fields.
Changing the solidification cooling rate can control thermal-expansion mismatch and the resulting residual-stress fields.
Residual-stress fields arise from differential contraction among compositional constituents during solidification.
Rapid cooling produces significant temperature gradients and local contraction differences among the constituent elements.
Local contraction differences create inhomogeneous residual stresses.
The residual stresses enhance dislocation pinning.
The residual stresses influence dynamic precipitation during aging.
Dislocation pinning and precipitation effects associated with residual stress unify the alloy's creep resistance, microhardness changes, and thermoelastic behavior.
Slower, more uniform cooling will reduce thermal-mismatch residual stresses.
Slow-cooled samples will have lower creep resistance at 1250 °C than conventionally rapid-cooled samples.
Slow-cooled samples will show less pronounced hardness increases after deformation.
Slow-cooled samples will show less pronounced aging-induced hardening in the 600–800 °C range.
Slow-cooled samples will exhibit a modified temperature dependence of elastic moduli over 293–1100 K.
Conventionally rapid-cooled HfNbTaTiZr exhibits previously measured high-temperature creep resistance at 1250 °C.
Conventionally rapid-cooled HfNbTaTiZr exhibits previously measured cold-rolling microhardness changes.
Conventionally rapid-cooled HfNbTaTiZr exhibits previously measured elastic-modulus variation from 293 to 1100 K.
Conventionally rapid-cooled HfNbTaTiZr exhibits previously measured aging-induced hardening between 600 and 800 °C.

A failure of confirmed residual-stress reduction to produce systematic differences in creep behavior, elastic-modulus trends, microhardness, and aging hardening would falsify thermal-expansion mismatch as the governing mechanism.
